comments.author: Briskfall
comments.body:
The field looks burnt and "indie" -- if that's the look that you're going for. It has a "barebone" look to it where certain shaders are "off."

But yeah, you need to draw distance fog. It's a phenomenon that's often observed if you do photography. And implementing it well will make a game look more polished.

replies.author: Briskfall
replies.body:
Some people are fine with this look, while some other people aren't. It's an acquired taste thing. You don't have to implement it if you see nothing wrong with it. If you want to put work in acquiring a potentially bigger playerbase, then adding it might be worth it.

I'm not sure about your question, because I already explained the core of the problem. Are you asking about implementation method \[of distance fog\]? Or is the concept \[distance fog\] itself foreign to you? Since we all work with LLMs here , you can just bring it up to them, as they 1) know your code base and have full context 2) will do a better job at walking you through it.

There are different ways to go about it, and there are tradeoffs too (as it might make your game take a performance hit if done sloppily). Whether you think it's worth the effort is up to you.

comments.author: Salt-Freedom-2419
comments.body:
Looks good, especially in the last two images, but there's a weird lack of depth. I think it has something to do with the transition between the nearby hills and the horizon. The landscape doesn't quite feel like it stretches into the distance. Some clouds casting dynamic shadows across the terrain might also help break things up and make it feel less flat.

It might also help to change the perspective a bit and raise the camera, because right now the low quality of the distant terrain isn't doing you any favours.

I think part of the problem is that graphical realism is just really hard to pull off. The closer you get to photorealism, the more noticeable the things that *aren't* realistic become. You're basically setting an expectation that every part of the image has to live up to, and when something doesn't, it creates this weird disconnect. The player stops seeing a coherent game world and starts noticing the graphical shortcomings instead.

Sometimes it's actually better to lean a little into the fact that it's a game. A subtle grid, some colorful icons, slightly stylized terrain, or other deliberate visual elements can help establish a more consistent aesthetic. You're no longer asking the player to judge the world against reality, but against its own visual language. And that gives you a lot more room to work with.

Aside from that, it has a really solid Western vibe. Really cool.
